<reason>A built a falsifiable trigger (full employment → primary balance, "paid for" not merely "sounds productive") and used the pressure round to expose that B never offered any threshold at which its "grow out of it" framework would ever recommend restraint. A's rebuttals dismantled B's core analogies precisely: the WWII case relied on demobilization, favorable demographics, and negative real rates that don't exist today, and the Eurozone case relied on recession-era austerity that the motion never demands. A's mortgage/credit-line analogy sharpened the stock-vs-flow dispute effectively. B's denominator/growth argument and the "escape hatch" charge were genuinely strong and forced A to clarify its bar in Rebuttal 2, but B's own answer to the threshold question dodged into "no single ratio" and redefined tax cuts/benefit expansions as "legacy law" rather than new commitments — a definitional move A punished cleanly in closing by noting that unfunded extension is itself a fresh choice. B's closing claim that A "never rebutted" the growth mechanism "not once in five speeches" overstates the record and weakens B's credibility. A's closing frame ("can either side's rule ever say no?") crystallized the decisive asymmetry more memorably than B's restated denominator point. Both sides suffered clipped speeches, but A's clipped material was mostly summary flourish, while the core arguments were intact and better resolved.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 1 dismantling of the WWII/Eurozone analogies (A2.1–A2.4), combined with A's Rebuttal 2 exposure that B never answered the threshold question raised in Pressure Questions (A4.6–A4.7), forms the most decisive exchange: it forced B into an unfalsifiable-sounding "dynamic" standard that A then weaponized in closing.</best_rebuttal>
